newsitem.title: CANADA: Detective asks Canadian Nazis to rat on comrades.
newsitem.headline: Detective asks Canadian Nazis to rat on comrades.

text.p: Jewish activists on Wednesday challenged Nazi war criminals living in Canada to turn in evidence against their Second World War comrades or risk being fingered themselves.

"If you are a war criminal this is your last chance, because if you don't come forward and cooperate with us, we may very well end up building a case against you with another cooperative witness," said detective Steve Rambam.

Rambam is an American investigator who won prominence over the last few months by announcing he had interviewed 58 alleged war criminals in Canada, including a Lithuanian who described how Jews were mowedn down into a trench built for that purpose.

He told a joint news conference with the Canadian Jewish Congress (CJC) that he and his colleagues had decided the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) had not acted in good faith with information he had turned over 90 days ago.

Therefore he said that in conjunction with the CJC he would be pursuing independent investigations and undertaking to ask the government for special treatment for any war criminals who inform on their co-conspirators.
He asserted that two people had already made preliminary offers to come forward.

CJC War Crimes Committee Chairman Irving Abella called on Ottawa to make a public accounting for its efforts to find war criminals in the 10 years since the Deschenes Commission recommended looking at 224 cases, 20 of them urgently.
"In those 10 years, we have successfully deported one person. That is an awful record," he said.
Rambam charged that Canada was sheltering 1,000 to 3,000 Nazi war criminals.

Justice Minister Allan Rock, asked about that by Member of Parliament Val Meredith, replied: "Before the honourable member becomes misled by claims of thousands of cases where action should be taken, I want her to bear in mind that the Deschenes commission ... identified far fewer cases."
The Liberal government has begun cases against 10 alleged war criminals and was to begin two more by the end of March.
"We are not stopping at 12," he said.

But in an apparent reference to Rambam's refusal to cooperate further with the RCMP, he appealed: "If there are those, whoever they may be, who have evidence that is relevant to this matter, I urge them to turn that evidence over to the RCMP so that it can be evaluated and acted upon."
Responding to Abella's call for an audit, he told reporters later that what was more important than adding up lawyers' receipts was moving actual cases through the courts.
